questions.correct: A system always in exactly one state, changing by rules
wrong: A machine that runs many states at the same time
A motor that only ever spins at full power
A sensor that measures the robot's heading angle
questions.explain: A state machine is always in exactly one state and only changes by allowed rules — like a traffic light that's red, yellow, OR green, never two at once.

questions.q: The intake has which three states?
wrong: RED, YELLOW, and GREEN
LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH
LEFT, RIGHT, and CENTER
questions.explain: The intake's states are FORWARD (pulling in), OFF (stopped), and REVERSE (pushing out). It's always in exactly one of them.

questions.correct: A tiny custom type with only the values you name
wrong: A number that counts up every single loop
A motor command that sets a power level
A wire connecting the hub to the intake
questions.explain: An enum is a small custom type whose only values are the ones you list, like State { FORWARD, OFF, REVERSE }. It keeps the state to legal values only.

questions.q: What do the commands forward(), off(), and reverse() actually change?
questions.correct: Only the state field, not the motor directly
wrong: The motor's power level, skipping the state
The telemetry line on the Driver Hub
The robot's heading read from the IMU
questions.explain: Commands only change the state field — they decide. update() is what reads the state and drives the motor. Deciding and doing are kept separate.

questions.q: What does update() do each loop?
questions.correct: Makes the motor match the current state
wrong: Changes the state to the next one
Prints the state onto the telemetry
Reverses the two left drive motors
questions.explain: update() reads the state field and sets the motor to match — FORWARD power, zero, or REVERSE power. It runs every loop so the motor always matches the state.

questions.q: Why split the commands from update()?
questions.correct: Deciding what to do is kept separate from doing it
wrong: It makes the intake motor spin much faster
The rules require you to write two methods
It saves battery by skipping the run loop
questions.explain: Commands decide (set the state); update() does (drives the motor). Splitting them keeps the logic clean and means one place controls the hardware.

questions.q: What Java structure handles "one behavior per state"?
questions.correct: A switch statement on the state
wrong: A for loop counting up to the state
An import at the top of the file
A telemetry line printing the state
questions.explain: A switch (state) block gives each state its own case — FORWARD sets full power, OFF sets zero, REVERSE sets a gentle negative power.

questions.correct: Reacting to a button press, not to it being held
wrong: Reacting to a button the whole time it is held
Measuring how hard the button is being pressed
Detecting the edge of the field's perimeter wall
questions.explain: Edge detection fires on the moment of a press, not while held. Without it, a single press held for a few loops would toggle the intake many times.

questions.q: Which line detects a fresh A press?
wrong: gamepad1.a == true always
gamepad1.a || previousA
!gamepad1.a && previousA
questions.explain: pressedA = gamepad1.a && !previousA is true for exactly one loop — when A is down now but wasn't last loop. Then you save previousA = gamepad1.a.

questions.q: If a single button press toggles the intake many times...
questions.correct: Edge detection is missing (no previousA memory)
wrong: The battery voltage is far too low
The intake motor is wired backward
The telemetry update is being skipped
questions.explain: The loop runs ~50 times a second, so a held press flips the state every loop unless you use edge detection to fire only on the press.

questions.q: Where must the previousA memory variable live?
questions.correct: Outside the loop, so it survives each pass
wrong: Inside the loop, resetting on every pass
Inside an import line at the very top
After the class's final closing brace
questions.explain: previousA must persist between loops to compare "now" against "last loop," so declare it outside the run loop where its value is kept.

questions.q: Why is only one state field the "source of truth"?
questions.correct: So the intake can't do two things at once
wrong: So the motor spins at twice the speed
So the battery drains a lot slower
So telemetry prints two lines at once
questions.explain: One field always says what the intake is doing. That prevents impossible situations — it can't be pulling in and pushing out at the same time.

questions.correct: Its update() never runs, so the motor never moves
wrong: The whole program refuses to build at all
The intake spins at full power forever
The robot drives in a slow steady circle
questions.explain: The scheduler only calls update() on subsystems in its list. Miss the add and update() never runs — your commands change the state but nothing moves.

questions.q: A typical FORWARD power for the intake is...
questions.correct: 1.0, full power to pull pieces in
wrong: 0.0, which means fully stopped
-1.0, which means full reverse
50, measured on a percent scale
questions.explain: INTAKE_FORWARD_POWER is around 1.0 (full inward), while REVERSE is a gentler negative like -0.5 to un-jam. OFF is 0.0.

questions.q: What happens if you reach the private motor from the OpMode?
questions.correct: It breaks encapsulation, which the design avoids
wrong: It makes the intake spin much faster
It charges the battery a little bit
It adds a telemetry line all by itself
questions.explain: The motor is private so only the subsystem drives it. Reaching in from outside breaks encapsulation — the whole point of commands like forward() and off().
